title: Kubernetes Fundamentals
description: Learn Kubernetes architecture, workloads, networking, and core operational concepts

questions.question: What is Kubernetes primarily used for?
options: Orchestrating and managing containerized applications at scale
Serving as a programming language for cloud-native apps
questions.explanation: Kubernetes is a container orchestration platform that automates deployment, scaling, networking, and lifecycle management for containerized workloads.

questions.question: What is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes?
questions.explanation: A Pod is the smallest deployable object in Kubernetes. It can run one or more closely related containers that share networking and storage.

questions.question: Which Kubernetes component stores the cluster's source-of-truth state?
questions.explanation: etcd is the distributed key-value store that persists Kubernetes cluster state, configuration, and metadata.

questions.question: What does the kube-scheduler do?
options: Assigns newly created Pods to suitable nodes
questions.explanation: The kube-scheduler watches for unscheduled Pods and selects a node for each Pod based on resource requirements, policies, and placement rules.

questions.question: Which component runs on each worker node and makes sure containers described by Pod specs are running?
questions.explanation: The kubelet is the node agent. It communicates with the control plane and ensures the containers defined for Pods on that node are running properly.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a Deployment?
options: To manage stateless application rollouts and maintain desired replicas
questions.explanation: A Deployment declaratively manages stateless applications by creating ReplicaSets, maintaining the desired number of replicas, and supporting rolling updates and rollbacks.

questions.question: What does a ReplicaSet ensure?
options: That every node has the same operating system
That a specified number of Pod replicas are running
That external DNS records stay synchronized
That containers share the same filesystem
questions.explanation: A ReplicaSet keeps the desired number of matching Pods running. If a Pod fails, the ReplicaSet creates a replacement.

questions.question: What does a ClusterIP Service provide?
options: Direct public internet access from every Pod
An internal virtual IP for accessing a set of Pods inside the cluster
A persistent disk for stateful workloads
questions.explanation: ClusterIP is the default Service type. It exposes an application on an internal cluster IP so other workloads inside the cluster can reach it reliably.

questions.question: How does a NodePort Service expose an application?
options: By turning each Pod into its own load balancer
By creating a VPN tunnel to the control plane
By writing traffic rules directly into etcd
By opening the same static port on each node's IP address
questions.explanation: A NodePort Service exposes the application on a port of every node, allowing external clients to access the Service through any node IP and that port.

questions.question: What kind of data should typically be stored in a ConfigMap?
options: Non-sensitive configuration such as feature flags or application settings
questions.explanation: ConfigMaps are designed for non-sensitive configuration data, such as environment-specific settings, command-line arguments, or configuration files.

questions.question: Why would you use a Secret instead of a ConfigMap?
options: Secrets are intended for sensitive values such as passwords, tokens, and keys
Secrets can only be used by StatefulSets
Secrets replace Services for secure networking
questions.explanation: Secrets are used for sensitive information. They help separate confidential data from regular configuration and can be handled with stricter access controls.

questions.question: What problem do Namespaces solve in Kubernetes?
options: They create new worker nodes automatically
They encrypt all traffic between Pods
They provide logical isolation and organization for resources in the same cluster
They convert stateless applications into stateful ones
questions.explanation: Namespaces let teams organize and isolate resources within one cluster, which is useful for separating environments, applications, or teams.

questions.question: What happens during a rolling update managed by a Deployment?
options: All Pods are deleted before any new ones are created
The cluster is restarted node by node
Only etcd is updated while workloads stay the same
Old Pods are replaced gradually with new Pods to reduce downtime
questions.explanation: Rolling updates replace Pods incrementally so the application can stay available while a new version is introduced.

questions.question: Why is a Kubernetes Service commonly used in front of Pods?
options: It provides a stable endpoint and load balancing for a changing set of Pods
It compiles YAML manifests into binaries
questions.explanation: Pods are ephemeral and their IP addresses can change. A Service gives clients a stable way to reach the application and can distribute traffic across multiple Pods.

questions.question: What is the job of the container runtime on a Kubernetes node?
options: To schedule Pods across the cluster
To pull images and run containers on the node
To expose Services with external IP addresses
questions.explanation: The container runtime, such as containerd, is responsible for fetching images and running containers on the node as instructed by the kubelet.

questions.question: What does kube-proxy primarily handle?
options: Implementing Service networking and forwarding traffic to Pods
questions.explanation: kube-proxy maintains network rules on each node so traffic sent to a Service can be forwarded to one of the matching backend Pods.

questions.question: Which component is the main API entry point for Kubernetes?
questions.explanation: The kube-apiserver exposes the Kubernetes API and serves as the front door for users, automation, and internal cluster components.

questions.question: Which workload type is best suited for applications that need stable network identities and persistent storage?
questions.explanation: StatefulSets are designed for stateful applications that need stable Pod identities, ordered rollout behavior, and persistent storage.

questions.question: What is a PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) used for?
options: To expose a Deployment over HTTPS
To request storage resources for a workload
To limit CPU and memory on a Pod
questions.explanation: A PersistentVolumeClaim is a storage request made by a workload. Kubernetes uses it to bind the workload to suitable persistent storage.

questions.question: What does a DaemonSet ensure?
options: Exactly one control plane per namespace
A copy of a Pod runs on every matching node
questions.explanation: A DaemonSet is used for node-level agents, such as log collectors or monitoring agents, by ensuring a Pod runs on every relevant node.

documentation:
Kubernetes Fundamentals

Kubernetes is an open-source container orchestration platform used to deploy, scale, and manage containerized applications. It helps teams run applications reliably across clusters of machines instead of managing individual containers by hand.

Cluster Architecture

A Kubernetes cluster is split into a control plane and worker nodes.

  • Control plane: Makes global decisions about the cluster and maintains the desired state.
  • Worker nodes: Run the application workloads inside Pods.

Key Control Plane Components

  • kube-apiserver: The front door to the cluster. All API requests pass through it.
  • etcd: Distributed key-value store that holds cluster state and configuration.
  • kube-scheduler: Chooses a suitable node for each unscheduled Pod.
  • kube-controller-manager: Runs controllers that continuously reconcile actual state with desired state.

Key Worker Node Components

  • kubelet: Node agent that ensures Pods are running as defined.
  • kube-proxy: Maintains networking rules for Services and traffic forwarding.
  • Container runtime: Pulls images and runs containers on the node.

Core Kubernetes Objects

  • Pod: Smallest deployable unit, containing one or more containers that share networking and storage.
  • Deployment: Manages stateless application releases, scaling, rolling updates, and rollbacks.
  • ReplicaSet: Keeps the required number of matching Pods running.
  • StatefulSet: Manages stateful applications that need stable identities and persistent data.
  • DaemonSet: Ensures a Pod runs on every matching node, often for logging or monitoring agents.
  • Job/CronJob: Runs finite or scheduled tasks rather than long-lived services.

Networking and Service Discovery

Pods are replaceable, so their IP addresses can change. Kubernetes Services provide stable access to groups of Pods.

  • ClusterIP: Internal-only Service accessible within the cluster.
  • NodePort: Exposes the Service on a static port on each node.
  • LoadBalancer: Requests an external load balancer from the infrastructure provider.
  • ExternalName: Maps a Service to an external DNS name.

Configuration and Secrets

  • ConfigMap: Stores non-sensitive configuration such as flags, endpoints, and settings.
  • Secret: Stores sensitive data such as passwords, API tokens, and certificates.
  • Namespace: Organizes and isolates resources in the same cluster for teams, apps, or environments.

Storage

Containers are often ephemeral, but many applications need durable data.

  • PersistentVolume (PV): Represents storage available to the cluster.
  • PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC): A workload's request for storage.
  • Volumes: Mount storage into Pods so data can survive container restarts.

Application Lifecycle

  • Desired state: You declare what you want, and controllers work to keep the cluster in that state.
  • Rolling updates: Deployments gradually replace old Pods with new ones to reduce downtime.
  • Self-healing: Failed Pods can be recreated automatically by controllers such as Deployments and ReplicaSets.
  • Scaling: Replica counts can be adjusted to handle changing demand.

Why Kubernetes Matters

Kubernetes standardizes how teams package, deploy, and operate modern applications. It improves portability, supports automation, and helps applications stay available even as underlying containers and nodes change.
